title: Preoperative and Postoperative Carcinoembryonic Antigen as Predictors of Outcome in Distal Colorectal Cancer: A Single-Center Retrospective Study
content: Background: In colorectal cancer (CRC), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is widely used for phasing and postoperative observation. However, the ability of perioperative CEA levels to predict outcomes, particularly in distal CRC, remains under discussion. In this study, the prognostic value of preoperative and postoperative CEA levels is evaluated in patients having distal colorectal cancer undergoing curative resection. . Methods: In this single-center retrospective study, patients with histologically proofed distal colorectal adenocarcinoma who took curative-intent surgery between January 2015 and December 2020 were included. Preoperative CEA was measured within four weeks prior to surgery, whereas postoperative CEA was defined as the first surveillance value obtained between 3 and 6 months after surgery. 5 ng/mL was used as a cut-off value. Disease recurrence was defined as the primary outcome followed by the overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS) as secondary outcomes. Results: A total of 231 patients, 61% of whom were male, with a median age of 62 years, participated in the study. Elevated preoperative CEA levels (≥5 ng/mL) were observed in 20.3% of patients and were significantly associated with advanced T stage (T4: 17.8% vs. 4.8%, p = 0.006). Patients with elevated preoperative CEA had higher recurrence rates (25.5% vs. 12.0%, p = 0.019) and shorter DFS (48 vs. 54 months, p = 0.033). Overall survival did not differ significantly between groups (p = 0.912). Among patients who developed recurrence, elevated CEA levels at the time of recurrence were significantly associated with worse OS (p = 0.008). Conclusions: In patients with distal colorectal cancer, elevated preoperative CEA is associated with advanced tumor stage and shorter disease-free survival, while CEA elevation at the time of recurrence is a strong predictor of poor overall survival. These findings support the continued role of perioperative and longitudinal CEA monitoring in risk stratification and postoperative surveillance of distal CRC.
